title: Thirteen hours, no breaks
topic: Rotas, leave, and training versus service
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in intensive care. It is 22:30, and you have just finished a 13-hour shift without a single break because the unit was so busy. Your next shift starts at 07:30 tomorrow.

This is the third time in two weeks this has happened. You feel exhausted.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Accept it as part of working in intensive care.
options.detailed: Intensive care is demanding, but missing all breaks and minimum rest repeatedly isn't safe or acceptable.

options.text: Phone in sick tomorrow to get some rest.
options.brief: Not honest unless you are unwell, and leaves the unit short.
options.detailed: If you're too tired to work safely, you should say so honestly rather than call in sick.

options.text: Submit an exception report for the missed breaks and short rest.
options.brief: Exception reports record unsafe working so it can be addressed.
options.detailed: Missed breaks and less than the minimum rest between shifts are exactly what exception reports are for. They alert your supervisor and the guardian of safe working hours.

options.text: Have strong coffee before your next shift and carry on.
options.detailed: Caffeine may help briefly, but it doesn't make you safe after inadequate rest, and the problem will continue.

options.text: Raise the pattern with the guardian of safe working hours.
options.brief: A repeated pattern suggests a rota problem that needs fixing.
options.detailed: Three times in two weeks suggests a problem with staffing or the rota. Raising it with those responsible means it can be looked at.

options.text: Arrange to swap tomorrow's shift informally with a colleague who is less tired.
options.brief: May leave a colleague tired, and doesn't fix the rota.
options.detailed: Swaps can help, but informal swaps bypass the rota and don't address the pattern.

options.text: Be honest with the consultant tomorrow about how tired you are.
options.brief: Patients' safety depends on you being fit to work.
options.detailed: If you are too fatigued to make safe decisions, the consultant needs to know so they can support you. This is a professional responsibility, not a weakness.

options.text: Post about the conditions on social media to raise awareness.
options.brief: Bypasses routes that can fix the problem.
options.detailed: Public awareness has its place, but posting online won't fix your rota and could identify colleagues or patients.

explanation.issue: This tests how you respond to unsafe working patterns, protecting patients and yourself through proper routes.
explanation.keyDetails: No breaks in 13 hours, and less than the minimum rest before your next shift. It has happened repeatedly. You are exhausted.
explanation.reasoning: [C] records it, [E] addresses the pattern, and [G] protects patients tomorrow. The distractors accept it ([A], [D]), are dishonest ([B]), bypass proper routes ([F]), or go public ([H]).
explanation.competing: [F] is the tempting option, as swaps can help, but an informal swap doesn't fix the rota and may tire a colleague.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 1, making sure fatigue doesn't put patients at risk.
